name: Plasma pen eyelid lift

card.summary: A handheld plasma-arc device used to tighten eyelid skin without a scalpel; popular online, with no cosmetic trials found.
card.note: No clinical studies of the cosmetic eyelid use were found; cheap consumer devices are sold alongside clinic treatments.

quick.overview:
A plasma pen creates a small electrical arc that ionizes gas near the skin. Online, it is promoted as a non-surgical way to tighten droopy eyelids and treat wrinkles, with the eyelid, nasal folds, forehead and neck named as common sites.
No clinical trials of plasma pens for eyelid lifting have been published. Related published work involves medical or laboratory uses of plasma, such as a case report using a plasma pen on a periocular xanthogranuloma.
quick.mechanism: Proponents describe the arc as creating tiny points of tissue damage that tighten skin as it heals. This is the community's explanation; no trial confirming it was found.
quick.risks: Forum posts describe both home devices (about $40 to $60) and clinic treatments ($400 to $1,900) [1]. The eyelid is next to the eye, and no safety data for cosmetic eyelid use were found. Research plasma devices of related type are tested in labs and in medicine, not as eyelid lifts.

lead: A plasma pen eyelid lift (also called fibroblast plasma treatment, plasma exeresis, plasma sublimation or "soft surgery") is a cosmetic procedure in which a handheld device produces a small plasma arc near the skin, with the stated aim of tightening upper and lower eyelid skin without a scalpel. People use it to reduce the look of hooded or crepey eyelids and to give the eye area a tighter, more open appearance, which they say improves overall facial impression [1][21].

The procedure covers a wide range. In clinics it is performed with medical plasma devices whose use on the eyelids has been described in small published studies since 2018. Online, the same idea is sold through inexpensive consumer pens and through beauty-salon treatments, and discussion of those is where most social-media attention sits [10][7][22].

On looksmax.org, one guide recommends the pen for the eyelids, nasal fold areas, forehead and neck, and advises treating the whole eye area rather than isolated spots; it lists devices at roughly $40 to $60 and clinic treatments at $400 to $1,900 [1]. The practice spread through social media in the 2020s, where hashtags such as #PlasmaPen and #FibroblastPlasma drew attention from dermatology researchers [7].

Published clinical work on plasma devices for eyelid skin consists of small studies of 10 to 56 participants, mostly in women with mild to moderate lid laxity, reporting improvement in laxity scores [10][12][13][15][16]. Case reports have also documented burns and an eye injury linked to plasma fibroblast treatments [9][14].

chain: Pen creates a small plasma arc at the skin surface
Proponents say the arc contracts and resurfaces the treated skin
Tighter-looking eyelid skin and a more open eye area
angle.text: Users and practitioners apply tiny plasma dots to eyelid skin, aiming for a tighter, lifted look without surgery. Proponents describe it as a middle option between topical products and blepharoplasty.

infobox: Handheld plasma arc / plasma exeresis device
Fibroblast pen, plasma fibroblast, plasma sublimation, soft surgery [1][7]
Many commercially sold pens are not FDA-regulated [7]

paras: Plasma, sometimes called the fourth state of matter, can be produced as thermal or non-thermal (cold atmospheric) plasma, and cold plasma has been studied in biomedicine for disinfection [3]. The cosmetic devices discussed here are different: a handheld tip passes a small electrical arc across a gap to the skin, and the energy creates tiny points of thermal change rather than cutting [18].

Treatment is described as placing a pattern of small dots across the area, which proponents say makes the skin contract and, as it heals, look tighter. Clinical authors use the terms plasma exeresis and plasma sublimation for the clinic version, and describe it as one of several non-surgical blepharoplasty techniques alongside fillers, lasers, platelet-rich plasma and threads [21][22][13].

Plasma pens used in cosmetics are marketed to the public alongside separate medical and veterinary plasma devices, and the two are distinct categories. A 2022 analysis of TikTok content describes fibroblast pens as marketed for a range of skincare benefits and notes that many pens sold commercially and shown in videos are not FDA-regulated [7].

Surgical blepharoplasty removes or repositions excess eyelid skin and fat and may reinforce underlying tissue; upper-lid surgery is done for appearance or to restore vision blocked by sagging skin, and lower-lid surgery can be done through the skin or the inner eyelid [8]. Recovery is usually outpatient, with swelling and bruising that fade over several weeks [8]. The term blepharoplasty dates to 1818, when Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coined it, and a Roman author, Celsus, described eyelid skin excision in the first century [8]. Plasma pen treatment is promoted as a non-surgical alternative to this category, although Wikipedia's blepharoplasty article does not discuss plasma devices [8].

Published studies of plasma devices on eyelids are small and mostly use clinic-grade devices. A 2018 pilot of plasma exeresis for upper eyelid skin treated 10 patients in three interventions; clinical improvement averaged 2.6 points on a facial laxity scale, confocal imaging showed collagen as long straight fibers in all cases, and no serious adverse events were reported [10].

A 2021 observational study of 16 patients (mean age 50.5, mostly women) found satisfaction highest at day 7; the authors described overall satisfaction as questionable because fewer patients would repeat the procedure and expectations declined over time. Eyelid edema was the most reported symptom at 7 days and itching at 30 days [11].

A 2022 clinical trial of 56 women with mild-to-severe dermatochalasis and periorbital wrinkles reported significant improvement in dermatochalasis and palpebral laxity versus baseline, most participants relatively satisfied, and no significant or permanent side effects [12]. A 2022 trial of 40 women, each treated in three sessions one month apart, reported lower Facial Laxity Rating Scale scores in 36 of 40 (90 percent), no change in 4, and no serious adverse events [13].

A 2020 study of 10 patients given two sessions 30 days apart using plasma radiofrequency ablation described the aesthetic results as optimal and reported no adverse effects, without quantitative measures in the abstract [17]. In 2024, a study of 21 women with lateral dermatochalasis treated with ablative radiofrequency microplasma found that greater severity went with greater improvement; the authors suggested microplasma suits grades 0 and 1, while surgery gives better results for advanced grades [16]. A 2025 study with a porcine stage and a clinical trial of 13 patients reported improved Dermatochalasis Scale and Global Aesthetics Improvement Scale scores and no serious adverse events [15].

Related work includes a 2022 histology study of a handheld plasma device in two subjects (pre-auricular and upper eyelid skin), which found device power significantly affected wound depth and width but not thermal spread [18]; a 2024 retrospective series of 71 eyes treated with plasma exeresis for benign eyelid lesions, with satisfied patients and temporary mild irritation in three [19]; and a 2025 series of six women using plasma-based Müller's muscle sublimation for mild to moderate ptosis, with margin reflex distance improving from 1.58 to 3.66 mm at 6 months [20]. These studies concern clinic-grade devices; none tested inexpensive consumer pens.

A looksmax.org thread presents the plasma pen as a way to get tighter skin, an improved eye area and better skin overall, naming the eyelids as the most common treatment site and arguing that skin quality drives appearance [1]. A reply says the poster would get it when under-eyes decline, and the author answered that the whole eye area should be treated [1].

A 2022 analysis of TikTok posts under four plasma and fibroblast pen hashtags found that 36 percent of creators were lay users and 25 percent described themselves as fibroblast skin-tightening specialists; 61 percent of posts were advertising, 26 percent personal experience, 6.5 percent education and 6.5 percent warnings, most of the warnings coming from medical doctors [7].

The 2022 TikTok analysis lists potential adverse effects including dyspigmentation, scarring and mechanical burns of the skin [7]. A 2024 case report in Cureus described a second-degree burn over the breast after an attempted tightening with a PlasmaPen, a procedure the authors said had been popularised on social networks [9]. A 2020 case report described bilateral alkali chemical eye injuries after plasma fibroblast skin tightening, which the authors attributed to inadvertent ocular exposure to numbing cream used before the procedure; the patient recovered with topical antibiotics [14].

In clinic studies, reported effects were generally transient, such as edema, itching, tenderness and mild irritation, with no serious adverse events [10][11][13][19]. The eyelid region is close to the eye, and no study has assessed cosmetic use of consumer pens there.

A 2025 case report described plasma pen ablation for extensive periocular xanthogranuloma, a medical rather than cosmetic use [2]. Laboratory studies have tested cold plasma pens on cancer cell lines using plasma-activated liquids [5] and on pathogens from canine keratitis [4]; an earlier study tested tissue-tolerable plasma on pig eyes as an antiseptic [6]. These are not tests of eyelid tightening.

TikTok launches; fibroblast pens later spread widely on the platform [7].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the plasma pen is presented as an inexpensive eyelid and skin-quality upgrade [1].

claims.claim: A plasma pen can give "baby-skin" and a better eye area.
claims.believers: The thread author says the pen simulates and rejuvenates sagging, wrinkled skin and that treating eyelids and other spots can improve overall looks [1].
claims.experts: Small clinic studies of plasma devices report improved laxity scores in the eyelid area [10][12][13]; one study described overall satisfaction as questionable [11]. Dermatology authors note potential dyspigmentation, scarring and burns from fibroblast pens [7].

claims.claim: A home device at $40 to $60 does what a $400 to $1,900 clinic treatment does.
claims.believers: The thread notes device and clinic price ranges and says the results are worth it [1].
claims.experts: No studies compare home devices with clinic treatments; published eyelid trials used clinic-grade devices, and many commercial pens are not FDA-regulated [7][12].

claims.claim: Plasma is a non-surgical substitute for blepharoplasty.
claims.believers: Proponents present the pen as a middle option between topical products and surgery [1].
claims.experts: The 2024 microplasma study suggested it suits mild laxity (grades 0 and 1), with surgery giving better results in advanced grades [16].

claims.claim: The whole eye area should be treated rather than isolated spots.
claims.believers: The thread author said the whole eye area should be treated [1].
claims.experts: The published studies treat the eyelid area as defined by their protocols; no study compares whole-area with spot treatment [10][13].

claims.claim: Treatment is safe and has no downtime.
claims.believers: Promoters on social media present it as simple and effective; only 6.5 percent of analysed TikTok posts were warnings [7].
claims.experts: Clinic studies report transient edema, itching and irritation [11][19]; case reports describe a burn and a chemical eye injury [9][14].
